clinicalPearls: Type 5 most often refers to the transient antenatal Bartter syndrome caused by X-linked MAGED2 mutations.
It presents with severe, early polyhydramnios and marked prematurity, frequently earlier and more severe than other antenatal Bartter subtypes.

The salt-wasting, polyuria and biochemical disturbance — a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with hyperreninaemia and hyperaldosteronism — characteristically resolve spontaneously within weeks of birth.
MAGED2 supports expression and trafficking of the NKCC2 and NCC cotransporters, a role that appears critical under the hypoxic conditions of fetal life.
Inheritance is X-linked, so the disorder affects males almost exclusively while female carriers are usually unaffected.
The transient course contrasts sharply with the persistent, lifelong salt-wasting of classic Bartter types 1 to 4.
An alternative use of the label denotes autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia from activating CASR mutations, giving a Bartter-like picture with hypocalcaemia and hypercalciuria.
Antenatal recognition matters because perinatal mortality from extreme prematurity is the principal risk despite the eventual resolution.
reference.pathophysiology: The form most often designated Bartter syndrome type 5 is a transient antenatal salt-wasting tubulopathy caused by loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked MAGED2 gene, whose product interacts with heat-shock chaperones to support expression and membrane trafficking of the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter NKCC2 of the thick ascending limb and the sodium-chloride cotransporter NCC of the distal tubule, a role that is especially critical under the hypoxic, cooler conditions of fetal life. Impaired salt reabsorption causes marked fetal polyuria with severe early polyhydramnios and premature delivery, renal sodium and chloride wasting, secondary activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; because the chaperone-dependent contribution of MAGED2 becomes dispensable after birth, transporter function is compensated postnatally and the phenotype characteristically remits within weeks. The condition affects males almost exclusively, in keeping with X-linked inheritance. An alternative use of the label type 5 denotes autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia caused by activating mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor gene CASR, in which the overactive receptor inhibits NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and suppresses parathyroid hormone, yielding a Bartter-like salt-wasting picture accompanied by hypocalcaemia and hypercalciuria.
additionalDifferentials: Other antenatal or neonatal Bartter subtypes (types 1, 2 and 4)
Gitelman syndrome, typically with later onset, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria
Congenital chloride diarrhoea, which also produces metabolic alkalosis but with diarrhoea
Cystic fibrosis with salt loss and alkalosis
Pseudo-Bartter from diuretic exposure or surreptitious vomiting
Autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia from activating CASR mutations
Other causes of severe polyhydramnios and prematurity
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes and blood gas confirming a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Urinary electrolytes showing salt-wasting, with urinary calcium excretion
Serum calcium, magnesium and parathyroid hormone to identify the CASR variant
Renal ultrasound to assess for nephrocalcinosis
Genetic testing for MAGED2, CASR and the other Bartter genes
redFlags: Extreme prematurity and its complications, the leading cause of mortality
Severe dehydration and haemodynamic instability from salt and water loss
Life-threatening electrolyte disturbance such as profound hypokalaemia and alkalosis
Salt-wasting that persists beyond the neonatal period, suggesting a non-transient subtype
reference.prognosis: Provided the infant survives the hazards of severe prematurity, the MAGED2-related salt-wasting and electrolyte disturbance typically resolve within the first weeks to months of life, with an excellent long-term renal outlook. Persistence beyond infancy should prompt reconsideration of the subtype.
pitfalls: Assuming lifelong therapy is required when the MAGED2 form remits, so that continued aggressive supplementation risks harm.
Confusing the type 5 nomenclature, which spans the MAGED2 transient antenatal form and the CASR gain-of-function Bartter-like syndrome.
Missing the diagnosis antenatally when severe polyhydramnios is the only early clue.
Overlooking hypocalcaemia and hypercalciuria that would point to the CASR variant.
management: Supportive sodium chloride, fluid and potassium replacement through the neonatal period, anticipating spontaneous resolution
Prostaglandin synthetase inhibition where symptoms are severe, with withdrawal as the tubulopathy resolves
Intensive neonatal management of severe prematurity and its complications
Antenatal monitoring of severe early polyhydramnios, with consideration of amnioreduction
Avoidance of unnecessary long-term therapy given the characteristically transient course
Reassessment of the genetic subtype if salt wasting persists beyond infancy
Genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance, with carrier assessment of female relatives
